summary: Describes how to add cryptographic signatures and encryption to MIME email data, which is what S/MIME is for. This is version 3. It was replaced by RFC 3851.

plainLanguage.summary: A way to seal an email in a signed, locked envelope so only the right person can open it and they know who sent it.

questions: how to sign and encrypt email
subtitle: How to add cryptographic signatures and encryption to MIME email messages.

tldr.problem: Email systems need a standard way to add cryptographic security services like authentication, integrity, and confidentiality to MIME messages.
tldr.mechanism: S/MIME (Secure MIME) defines how to use CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax, derived from PKCS #7) to create signed and encrypted MIME messages, including support for both multipart/signed (clear-signed) and application/pkcs7-mime (opaque) formats.
tldr.outcome: S/MIME v3 became a standards track protocol widely implemented in email clients and systems, though it has been superseded by RFC 3851 with security and interoperability improvements.

today: RFC 2633 defined S/MIME v3 as a Standards Track protocol and was widely implemented in email clients and servers. It has been superseded by RFC 3851, which provides updates for better security and interoperability with modern cryptographic practices and algorithms.

sections.title: Overview and Design Goals
sections.content:
S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) provides a consistent way to send and receive secure MIME data. Based on the MIME standard, S/MIME provides cryptographic security services for electronic messaging: authentication, message integrity and non-repudiation of origin (using digital signatures) and privacy and data security (using encryption).

S/MIME can be used by traditional mail user agents (MUAs) to add cryptographic security to mail sent and received, but is not restricted to mail. It can be used with any transport mechanism that transports MIME data, such as HTTP. S/MIME can also be used in automated message transfer agents that require cryptographic security without human intervention, such as signing software-generated documents or encrypting FAX messages sent over the Internet.

The design philosophy is to be liberal in what you receive and conservative in what you send. This means receiving agents should be flexible in handling messages, while sending agents should create messages conservatively to ensure proper interoperability. The document also separates requirements for receiving agents (mostly strict) from recommendations for sending agents (mostly flexible).
sections.plainLanguage: The rules for how to lock and unlock email, and how different email programs should work together.

sections.title: Cryptographic Message Structures
sections.content:
S/MIME uses CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax), which defines three main content types used in S/MIME: Data (the actual message content), SignedData (adds digital signatures), and EnvelopedData (adds encryption). The RFC defines requirements for algorithm support: all agents must support SHA-1 for digests and Diffie-Hellman for key encryption, while they should support MD5 (for backward compatibility), RSA (for signatures and encryption), and TripleDES (for symmetric encryption).

For content encryption, TripleDES is mandatory while RC2/40 (weak encryption with 40-bit key) is optional. The RFC provides detailed guidance on which algorithm to use when sending: if recipient capabilities are known, use those; if a previous encrypted message was received, use its algorithm; if unknown, use TripleDES as the strongest option.

S/MIME defines attributes that can be included with signatures, including signingTime (when the message was signed), SMIMECapabilities (what algorithms the sender supports), and SMIMEEncryptionKeyPreference (which certificate the sender prefers for replies). These attributes inform recipients about the sender's capabilities and preferences.
sections.plainLanguage: Different ways to lock something, and what kinds of locks all the programs need to understand.

sections.title: Creating and Preparing Messages
sections.content:
To create S/MIME messages, the MIME entity must first be prepared according to specific procedures: convert leaf parts to canonical form, apply appropriate transfer encoding, and ensure line endings are the canonical CR/LF pair. Canonicalization is critical for signatures: the message must be the same when verified as when signed.

For text messages, both line endings and character set must be canonicalized. Other MIME types typically have only one representation, though canonicalization details depend on the specific MIME type.

For signing using the multipart/signed format (clear-signed), all MIME entities must be 7-bit text to ensure they can pass through the Internet mail infrastructure. S/MIME implementations must be able to deal with binary MIME objects, but should use 7-bit transfer encoding to allow messages to be handled in any environment without modification.
sections.plainLanguage: Get the email ready in a standard way so that when you sign it and lock it, it stays the same when someone else opens it.

sections.title: Message Formats and MIME Types
sections.content:
S/MIME defines the application/pkcs7-mime MIME type for carrying CMS objects. This type is used for enveloped-only, signed-only (opaque), and signed-and-enveloped messages. The optional smime-type parameter indicates the security applied: enveloped-data, signed-data, or certs-only. Base-64 transfer encoding is typically used for these binary CMS objects.

For clear-signed messages, the multipart/signed format is preferred. This has two parts: the first contains the original message (viewable by non-S/MIME clients), the second contains the detached signature in application/pkcs7-signature format. Two required parameters identify it: protocol (always application/pkcs7-signature) and micalg (the message digest algorithm used).

An enveloped-only message provides confidentiality but not authentication or integrity. A signed-only message provides authentication and integrity. For messages that are both signed and encrypted, any combination of signed-only and encrypted-only formats may be nested. Optional name and filename parameters on application/pkcs7-mime indicate file extensions (.p7m for signed/enveloped, .p7s for signature, .p7c for certs-only) for compatibility with older systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Different ways to package a locked email so it can travel through the mail system.

sections.title: Certificate Management
sections.content:
To create S/MIME messages, an S/MIME agent must have access to certificates and corresponding secret keys. If an S/MIME agent needs to generate a key pair, it must generate separate Diffie-Hellman and DSS public/private key pairs, each from a good source of non-deterministic random input. The agent should also support RSA key pair generation, with a minimum of 512 bits (though 768 bits or more is recommended for better security).

A receiving agent must provide some certificate retrieval mechanism to access certificates for message recipients. At minimum, an agent could automatically request a recipient's certificate in a signed return message. S/MIME agents should provide a mechanism to store and protect certificates for correspondents to guarantee their later retrieval.

The RFC notes that S/MIME v3 requires use of SignerInfo version 1 with issuerAndSerialNumber CHOICE for the SignerIdentifier. This ensures maximum interoperability with S/MIME v2 agents. Each key pair used with S/MIME must have corresponding certificates that can be validated according to PKIX procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: The email program needs special keys and certificates to sign and lock messages, and needs to know where to find keys for other people.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Operations
sections.content:
To create an enveloped-only message, prepare the MIME entity, process it into a CMS EnvelopedData object (encrypting the content-encryption key for each recipient and the originator), and wrap it in application/pkcs7-mime with smime-type=enveloped-data.

To create a signed message using the opaque format (application/pkcs7-mime with smime-type=signed-data), prepare the entity and process it into a CMS SignedData object, then wrap it in the MIME type. Alternatively, for clear-signed messages using multipart/signed, prepare the entity and obtain a SignedData object with no eContent field, then create a multipart/signed with the entity as the first part and the signature in application/pkcs7-signature as the second part.

To send a message that is both signed and encrypted, nest the formats: sign first then encrypt, or encrypt first then sign, depending on whether you want signatories hidden or signatures verifiable without decryption. A receiving agent must be able to handle arbitrarily nested S/MIME messages within resource limits. Signatures that fail validation should be treated as though they do not exist, and the message treated as unprotected.
sections.plainLanguage: The steps to lock a message, or sign it, or both, and what happens when someone receives it.
